headline: Cuba's power grid fails for the third time

sources.title: Cuba's power grid collapses again, triggering third blackout in 10 days
Analysis: Rocked by string of blackouts, Cubans' ability to endure reaches a limit
Cuba plunged into third nationwide blackout in two weeks as power grid collapses
Cuba slowly gets power back after third blackout in 10 days (video, France 24)

chunks.text: Cuba's national power [[grid]] has {{broken down}} [[yet again]]. On Tuesday, the whole island suddenly lost electricity, {{cutting off}} power for around 10 million people. It was the third major [[blackout]] in about two weeks. The Ministry of Energy said the system had completely {{shut down}}, and millions of families were left [[in the dark]] [[in the middle of]] the day.

verbs.wrong: To begin suddenly, like a fire
verbs.why: Break down means a machine or system suddenly stops working, whether it's a car, a printer, or an entire power grid. Cuba's grid broke down for the third time in two weeks.

verbs.wrong: To keep a place separate so that no one can reach it
verbs.correct: To stop the supply of something, like power or water
verbs.why: Cut off means to stop a supply completely, like power, water, or phone service. The failure cut off electricity for around ten million people at once.

verbs.wrong: To stop someone from entering a place
verbs.correct: To stop working or operating completely
verbs.why: Shut down means the whole system stops operating at once, not just one part of it. The Ministry said the entire grid had shut down that day.

chunks.text: The blackouts [[come from]] two deeper problems. First, the island is {{running out of}} fuel to power its plants, [[partly because of]] new US [[sanctions]] on countries that sell oil to Cuba. Second, many [[power stations]] are very old, built long ago in the 1960s and 1980s. On Tuesday, a single unit in the east of the country failed, and that quickly {{set off}} the wider [[collapse]].

verbs.wrong: To use something too quickly and waste it
verbs.correct: To have almost none of something left
verbs.why: Run out of means you have almost nothing left of something you need. Cuba is running out of the fuel its power plants need to work.

verbs.wrong: To begin a journey to a place
verbs.correct: To cause something to start or happen
verbs.why: Set off means one small event triggers something much bigger, like a spark starting a fire. A single failed unit set off the whole nationwide collapse.

chunks.text: [[Repair crews]] got to work [[right away]]. Engineers slowly {{turned on}} small 'islands' of electricity and then joined them together into a bigger network. Hospitals and food factories were the [[priority]], so workers {{dealt with}} them first. In the capital, Havana, teams began to {{bring back}} power before reaching [[the rest of]] the island.

verbs.wrong: To raise a machine's power to its highest level
verbs.correct: To start a machine or make power flow
verbs.why: Turn on means to start a machine or let electricity flow through it. Engineers turned on small sections of the grid one at a time before connecting them.

verbs.wrong: To decide which building gets power first
verbs.correct: To take action to handle or fix something
verbs.why: Deal with means to take direct action to handle a problem instead of ignoring it. Crews dealt with hospitals and food factories first, since they mattered most.

verbs.wrong: To carry something home with you from a trip
verbs.correct: To make something work or exist again
verbs.why: Bring back means to restore something to how it was, so it works or exists again. Teams worked to bring back power to Havana before the rest of the island.

chunks.text: For [[ordinary]] Cubans, these blackouts make [[daily life]] very hard. Without power, people cannot cook, pump water, or {{log on}} to the internet, and many hospital [[surgeries]] were {{called off}}. Anger is [[growing]] as families {{put up with}} one [[outage]] after another. The government has promised to repair the system, but with fuel [[still short]], few people [[expect]] a quick end to the [[crisis]].

verbs.wrong: To start a computer or phone
verbs.correct: To sign in to a computer system
verbs.why: Log on means to sign in to a computer or network before you can use it. Without power, Cubans could not log on to the internet at all.

verbs.wrong: To move patients to another hospital
verbs.correct: To cancel something that was planned
verbs.why: Call off means to cancel a plan that was already scheduled to happen. Hospitals had to call off many surgeries once the power failed.

verbs.wrong: To get ready for a hard time that is coming
verbs.correct: To accept something unpleasant without complaining
verbs.why: Put up with means to accept something difficult without complaining, at least for now. Families are putting up with blackout after blackout with no end yet in sight.

mainIdea.s: Cuba's power grid failed for the third time in about two weeks, cutting power to about 10 million people. Old power stations and a fuel shortage caused the collapse.
mainIdea.why: This was the third blackout in about two weeks, cutting power for about 10 million people. The cause was a fuel shortage and old power stations, the story says.

mainIdea.s: Cuba's grid failed only because its power stations are old, and crews restored the whole island at once. Officials say fuel has already arrived, ending the crisis.
mainIdea.why: Close, but crews restored power in stages, joining small areas together, not the whole island at once. The article also says fuel is still short, so few people expect a quick end to the crisis.

mainIdea.s: Cuba announced a new plan to build solar stations across the island to cut down on future blackouts. The project will take years and will not fix the current crisis.
mainIdea.why: This is about a future plan for new solar power, not the blackout itself. The real story is about the power grid failing three times in about two weeks.

tf.s: Cuba's national power grid has broken down for the third time in about two weeks.
tf.why: The story says this was the third major blackout in about two weeks after the grid collapsed again.

tf.s: Engineers turned on power to the whole island all at once.
tf.why: Engineers slowly turned on small 'islands' of electricity and then joined them together, rather than powering the whole island at once.

tf.s: Officials called off the repairs and told people to wait a week.
tf.why: Repair crews got to work right away and began to bring back power, so the repairs were not called off.

tf.s: Hospitals and food factories were dealt with first when power came back.
tf.why: They were the priority, so workers dealt with them first before the rest of the island.

tf.s: The blackouts come from a fuel shortage and very old power plants.
tf.why: The story says the crisis comes from a lack of fuel and power stations built back in the 1960s and 1980s.

tf.s: Cubans could still log on to the internet easily during the blackouts.
tf.why: Without power, people cannot log on to the internet, so this is false.
